pages.text: Corundum is aluminium oxide, Al2O3, the alumina of the Bayer plant grown into a crystal. A little chromium makes it red, ruby; iron and titanium together make it blue, sapphire; any other colour is sapphire too. Ruby grows where limestone is baked to marble, as at Mogok in Burma: here in the skarns.
pages.title: Ruby and sapphire

pages.text: Sapphire crystallises from syenite, rock with too little silica for quartz, as in the corundum syenites of Bancroft, Ontario and the Ilmen Mountains: here, scattered in the syenite massifs.

Auguste Verneuil made the first gem corundum in 1902 by flame fusion. Alumina powder is tapped through an oxyhydrogen flame, melts at 2,050 °C and drips onto a pedestal, which is lowered as a boule, the poire, grows on it.
pages.title: Verneuil

pages.text: Four alumina, 500 mB of hydrogen and 250 mB of oxygen, superheated, give a sapphire boule; pure alumina grows colourless, as the boules for watch jewels and windows do. Oxygen comes from air: a centrifuge vat that spins neon out of 1,000 mB of air gives 209 mB of it.

Create's mechanical saw cuts a boule to four sapphire wafers. Sapphire is the substrate of the blue LED: gallium nitride grows on its face as on almost nothing else, so the LED chip takes a sapphire wafer (see Germanium, indium, gallium and cadmium).
pages.title: Sapphire wafers

pages.text: Most LED sapphire is now grown by Kyropoulos's method, a crystal cooled slowly in its crucible, but Verneuil's flame is the older road.

Ruby is a gem here and no more. Maiman's first laser of 1960 was a rod of synthetic ruby pumped by a flash tube, and ruby lasers have drilled watch jewels and diamond dies, but nothing in the pack wants a pulsed red laser: The Fab's 90 nm reticle writer is the kind that runs on a continuous ultraviolet laser.
pages.title: Ruby

pages.text: Sources: Verneuil, "Mémoire sur la reproduction artificielle du rubis par fusion", Annales de Chimie et de Physique 3 (1904); Dobrovinskaya, Lytvynov and Pishchik, Sapphire: Material, Manufacturing, Applications (Springer, 2009); Hughes, Ruby and Sapphire (RWH, 1997); Maiman, "Stimulated optical radiation in ruby", Nature 187 (1960).
